en: The *Yao shi jing shu* (Commentary on the Bhaisajyaguru-sutra) states: "The sixth is the Skandha of the Five Faculties (*pañcendriya-khandha*). The seventh is the Skandha of Concentration (*samādhi-khandha*).
The eighth is the Skandha of Vision (*darśana-khandha*). This person [referred to] is Śamathadatta. How is this known? The *Vibhāṣā* says:"
Śamathadatta was able to understand this meaning;
however, at that time he had entered meditative absorption and could not consult him.
After he had emerged from absorption, Kātyāyana composed the treatise.
The second is that six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five hundred arhats,
together with the master Kātyāyanīputra, composed the Vibhāṣā in one hundred sections.
*Vibhāṣā* means "the exposition by the assembly" (*zhòngshuō*).
It was expounded collectively by a great assembly of five hundred arhats.
This work provides an exegesis of the eight *skandhas*.
The *Jingnü wufen* explains the *Za jian-du*;
next, the *Nü wufen* explains the *Shi jian-du*;
and next, the *Shifen* explains the *Zhi jian-du*.
In total, there were sixty sections transmitted to this land;
the remaining forty sections, which explain the subsequent *khandakas*,
were lost during the turmoil in Liangzhou, and their original manuscripts did not arrive.
Furthermore, there is the *Vibhāṣā* in fourteen sections;
it does not record the names [of its authors] and appears to be an abridgment of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
In the second period, seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was a bhikṣu named Dharmatrāta who composed the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* (Four-Part Abhidharma).
Because the *Vibhāṣā* is so vast and difficult to investigate,
I have selected its essential expositions and composed two hundred and fifty verses, divided into four parts.
This refers to the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*.
It is called "Incomparable" because it elucidates the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that distinguishes the mundane from the supramundane, such that nothing can be compared to it.
The King presides over all the numerical categories, clarifying its four divisions and presiding over all the treatises.
In the fourth period, eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was Dharmatrāta, who composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in fourteen sections.
This refers to the teacher of the author of the treatise.
It is called "miscellaneous" (*saṃyukta*) because it elucidates numerous meanings rather than just a single one.
It is said that the *Vibhāṣā* is too extensive and difficult to consult.
The *Abhidharmadīpa* by Dharmottara was abridged and difficult to comprehend;
therefore, three hundred and fifty verses from the *Vibhāṣā* were taken to supplement Dharmottara’s work, bringing it to a total of six hundred verses.
Therefore, its text says:
"The extremely concise is difficult to understand;
the extremely extensive causes the intellect to recoil."
I now speak from a middle position,
adorning the meaning through extensive explanation;
this is not the "abridgment" of the Abhidharma, which is difficult to understand when abbreviated.
The *Viśālamati* causes one's wisdom to regress; the *Vibhāṣā* is excessively prolix.
These four treatises all belong to the Sarvāstivāda school, and they all clarify that one attains the Way through the perception of existence.
Next, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* appeared.
Some masters stated that it is a treatise of the Dharmaguptaka school.
Some claim it belongs to the Dārṣṭāntika school;

however, we maintain that this treatise does not specifically correspond to any single school, but rather draws extensively from the doctrines of various masters, adopting whichever interpretation is most excellent.
This was composed five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
There is a Dharma called the True Dharma (Saddharma).
Six hundred years after this, it will become the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma);
therefore, he says, "I vow [for the sake of] sentient beings of the future Semblance Dharma."
Furthermore, it should be known that five hundred years later, the Māra-king will appear in the world seeking to destroy the Buddha-dharma;
at that time, Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Āryadeva and others will further compose the Three Treatises.
To this day, the Three Jewels have remained uninterrupted;
because of these three great beings, Māra can no longer destroy the Buddha-dharma.
One thousand five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa will mark the beginning of the Final Dharma (mofa).
All the Mahāyāna sūtra-piṭakas have been taken away by the Dragon King.
The five corruptions (pañca-kaṣāya) arise and prevail.
As for the five corruptions:
First, the turbidity of the eon;
second, the turbidity of lifespan;
third, the turbidity of afflictions.
Fourth is the defilement of sentient beings;
fifth is the defilement of views.
Such defilements are indeed immeasurable.
On the other hand, for the sake of transformation, let us briefly speak of five kinds [of turbidities]:

the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), where various evils surge forth; the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), which brings about the destruction of the great kalpa through the incursions of barbarian armies and famine, engendering great terror among living beings.

Regarding the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): clinging to and cherishing this body, one deems it to be permanent; yet impermanence suddenly arrives, and death comes with no fixed time. It presses upon one until one reaches a state of dread and terror.
Regarding the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*):

Afflictions and entanglements bind and fetter the practitioner, causing them to revolve amidst forms and sounds and sink into the flow of fragrances and tastes; they commit evil with such intensity that they cannot reform themselves.
This refers to the "impurity of sentient beings" (sattva-kaṣāya).

Each of these is distinct: slandering the virtuous and good, being stingy with one's wealth, and being excessively greedy while seeking to carry out sensual desires; failing to choose between kin and the good, and slandering the three refuges.
Such manifold evils are likewise not to be enjoyed.
This is explained extensively in the *Śāstra*.
Regarding the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*):

they give rise to various false views, devoting themselves exclusively to serving celestial deities and supporting non-Buddhist practitioners; they seek merit through killing and commit evil to an even greater degree—this is a painful state that must be rescued.
At this time, those who wish to reach [this state] should exert their strength to proclaim and manifest it clearly.
Regarding those who abide in the names of the Buddhas of the past:
from here below is the second section, which inquires about the names of the Buddhas and their lands.
"We pray that you will explain it for us so that we may hear the essential points of the Dharma.
This is the third formal request.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
The following section is the second part, in which the Tathāgata answers the questions.
Within this response, there are generally two stages.
First, before answering, he praises [the questioner], saying "Excellent."
First there is the praise, next the command, and finally the permission.
Within the proclamation of the praise, the term "Excellent" (*sādhu*) is the general praise.
"Good" (*shan*) means "fine"; because the matter being praised is fine, it is called "Excellent."
This particle "shi" (是) serves as an auxiliary to bring forth the virtuous deeds of the various bodhisattvas in response to their questions and so forth.
As for the phrase "Your great compassion is immeasurable," this is the second answer, which addresses the previous point concerning the welfare of sentient beings.
The previous statement said, "I vow for the sake of sentient beings in the future age of semblance Dharma.
Now the answer says, "The reason you act for the sake of sentient beings is precisely because of your immeasurable compassion; therefore, I praise you, saying 'Excellent!'"
The question regarding the names of these past Buddhas is the third answer.
The second question proclaims and elucidates the names of the Buddhas of the past and the matters concerning the adornments of their pure lands.
The present answer says: "The reason you ask about the names of the Buddhas and their lands is not for your own sake, but solely for the sake of the bodies of sentient beings.
Listen attentively now."
Regarding this fourth section, the preceding summary request stated: "I pray that you will explain it so that I may hear the essentials of the Dharma.
Now, the answer is given: "If you truly must hear it, listen attentively now," thereby instructing him on how to establish the three types of wisdom (*tri-vidyā*).
Listen now attentively: the precept of a single dharma is for the sake of establishing the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Skillful reflection is for the sake of the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). The present teaching is for the sake of establishing the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Since you are now able to establish these three types of wisdom, [you shall attain liberation].
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
As for the assembly of bodhisattvas seated here:
this next section, second in order, clarifies how the gathered multitude yearns with longing. The Buddha said: "To the east of here, at a distance of ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges]."
From here below, the second section provides the direct answer to the preceding question.
Within this direct answer, there are generally three sections. The first concerns perception and mental formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra*).
The second is the single, extensive vow;
the third is the single, extensive practice.
Regarding the first—contemplating the manifestation of clarity and conduct—there are generally three stages.
First, he lists the names of the Buddhas of other directions,
thereby answering the aforementioned question regarding the names of those Buddhas.
Having thus set forth the names of the Buddhas, [the text continues].
The second [section] praises the virtues and deeds of that Buddha; the third briefly clarifies his practices and vows.
The first [section] clarifies the distance—ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [world-systems] to the east from this buddha-field—to that Buddha.
There is a Buddha named Bhaiṣajya.
The second line cites that Buddha’s name to answer Mañjuśrī:
"You asked me, saying..."
"I pray that you will speak the names of the Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings in the future age of semblance-dharma.
Now, in direct response to you, I say:
In this buddha-field, ten times as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a Buddha named Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.
Does this not answer the previous question?
The commentary states:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja" (Medicine King) is a name derived by borrowing a metaphor.

Just as a physician of the world can eliminate the internal diseases of humans, so too the Tathāgata, whose wisdom is luminous, can eliminate the three poisons, the four perversions, and all grave evils of sentient beings; by teaching them to practice the four immeasurables and the six perfections, he acts as a physician.

The "Lapis Lazuli Light" (Vairocana) is the lapis lazuli of the world, a treasure cherished within; it is luminous within and its fruit-body is endowed with myriad virtues, which is likened to lapis lazuli.
As for "light," it is that which can dispel darkness.
To clarify that the fruit of Buddhahood is fully endowed with the light of the dual understanding of emptiness and existence,
the tenth among the ten epithets is: first, *Tathāgata*.
In this region, he is translated as "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One);
he is also called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone One),
and also called "Tathāsthita" (Thus-Abiding One).
The Tathāgata is the Arhat-Buddha;
it is because of his compassion.
Because he comes to transform the triple world by means of the vehicle of *tathāgata-jñāna*, he is called the Tathāgata.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* states:
"First, the *nirmāṇa-buddha*'s *bodhi*: he manifests himself according to what ought to be seen by those to be converted."

As the sutras all state that the Tathāgata departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
therefore, this "Thus-Gone One" (Tathāgata) is the *nirmāṇakāya* (retribution Buddha).
Because one rides upon the path of reality as it is and attains the departure through the awakening of the mind, one is called the "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone).
The *Fahua lun* states:
"The second is the Bodhi of the Reward Buddha."
This means that because one attains the realization of eternal nirvana upon fulfilling the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is as the Sūtra says:
"Good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of *nayuta* kalpas have passed."
That which abides as suchness is the Dharma-Buddha.
Because it is eternally abiding and unchanging like the primordial suchness, it is called "abiding as suchness.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
Third is the Bodhi of the Dharma-Buddha, which refers to the Tathāgatagarbha being primordially pure, nirvāṇic, eternal, constant, pure, cool, and unchanging. As the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata, through his true suchness-knowledge and vision, perceives the characteristics of the triple world."
This is because they do not perceive the three realms as the three realms.
Second, the Arhat: in this region, he is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
He is also called "Arhat" (Killer of Thieves) and "Anutpāda" (Non-arising).
As for "Arhat," because the Tathāgata is worthy of receiving offerings from the world— including those of the two vehicles, humans, and devas— he is called "Arhat."
Because he is able to sever the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the five stages of dwelling, he is called a "slayer of thieves.
Because the sting of ignorance has been removed from his skin, he will not again undergo birth and death within the field of future lives; thus he is called "unborn" (*ajāta*).
One who possesses these three meanings is called an Arhat.
Third, as for Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the language of this region [China], it is translated as "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (Zhèngbiànzhī).
"Correct" means being distinct from the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
"Universal knowledge" means being distinct from those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Persons of the two vehicles both know that the Four Noble Truths are conditioned (saṃskṛta).
Because they do not know the four truths of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*),
they cannot be called "omniscient" (*sarvajña*).
This is because the Tathāgata knows both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
He is weighed as "omniscient";
therefore, he is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Fourth, *Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*:
in this land, the translation is "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."
"Knowledge" refers to the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
"Practice" refers to the three types of action (*karma*).
Regarding the person of the Hīnayāna, the clear knowledge of past lives pertains to the past.
The supernormal knowledge of the past knows only eighty thousand kalpas;
the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye regarding the future knows only eighty thousand kalpas;

and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows regarding the present knows only the exhaustion of the afflictions of the four abodes. Because these are not complete, they are not called "Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasampanna).
Even though the various bodhisattvas and others know the events of immeasurable Ganges-sand eons,
because they have not yet exhausted them,
it cannot be said that they are sufficient.
It is to clarify that because the Tathāgata has thoroughly mastered and exhausted the three periods of time, he is called "Complete" (*pūrṇa*).
Other practitioners have deficiencies in their three types of action (*trikarma*), and therefore they cannot be called complete;
only the Buddha is without deficiency, and thus he is called complete.
The fifth is Sugata; in this region, the translation of the name is "Good Vow" (Shanshi).
"Good" means excellent.
"Sworn" (praṇīta) means that the three types of departure are excellent.
Regarding "excellent departure," it is called excellent because one departs by mounting the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment.
Regarding "excellent teaching," it is called excellent because one teaches this true principle to sentient beings exactly as it is.
Because Śrāvakas have not attained ultimate departure, they are not called "Well-Gone" (Sugata).
Because they cannot deeply penetrate the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings to preach the Dharma for them, they are not called "Well-Spoken" (Sudeśaka).
The Tathāgata is first, because he profoundly penetrates the capacities of sentient beings;
second, because his departure is ultimate, he is called "Well-Gone" (Sugata). Sixth, regarding the addition of the spirit:
in this region, the translation for his title is "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
What are the three kinds of worlds?
First, the world of sentient beings;
second, the receptacle world.
Third is the world of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Regarding these,
the world of sentient beings is the primary retribution (*vipāka*),
while the receptacle world is the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
The "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is the one who understands the principles of the world.
Because he thoroughly and clearly knows these three kinds of worlds, he is called the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
The seventh, Anuttara, is translated in this region as "Unsurpassed One" (Wushangshi).
Why is he called the Unsurpassed One?
Among all sentient beings, the Buddha is supreme.
Among all phenomena, nirvana is supreme.
For what reason is the Buddha supreme?
Because it realizes the unsurpassed Dharma;
since the Dharma is unsurpassed, the person is also unsurpassed.
One must surely ask: for what reason is the Dharma unsurpassed?
Because he is a person who has realized the unsurpassed;
why is the person unsurpassed?
Because he has realized the unsurpassed Dharma, he is called an "unsurpassed person" (puruṣa). Eighth, *puruṣadamyasārathi* (the charioteer of persons to be tamed):
In this region, he is translated as "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).
There are five kinds of taming:
first, taming the people through official law.
Second, a father disciplines his son;
third, a teacher disciplines his disciples;
fourth, King Yama disciplines those who have committed offenses through their karma.
Among the five kinds of taming and guiding, the first three are taming and guiding in the present; the fourth is taming and guiding in future lives;
and the fifth is taming and guiding across all three periods of time because the tamer guides throughout the three times simultaneously.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra says:
"I have long established you before me and have already awakened you;
now I again receive you into my care."
It shall be so for your future births as well.
Therefore, it is known that the Buddha is the Tamer (Vināyaka) of the three periods of time.
The Buddha uses gentle speech and soft words.
Because he tames sentient beings through these three modes of speech, leading them out of birth and death, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi). Ninth, *śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām* means:
In this region, the name is translated as "Self-Heavenly-Man" (Zìtiānrén).
Why is it called "Teacher of Heaven and Men"?
It is because one wishes to clarify that the Tathāgata is the teacher of all sentient beings.
However, among the six realms of existence, gods and humans are the most excellent.
Because he teaches according to what is most excellent, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). "Buddha" is his tenth title.
In this region, he is translated as "The Awakened One" (Buddha).
What is meant by "The Awakened One"?
Because the Tathāgata, beneath the Bodhi tree, clearly and fully awakened to the knowledge of whether beings are sentient or non-sentient, he is called a Buddha.
Because he has long since awakened himself and awakened others, he is titled "Buddha.
He delivers those subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death;
this clarifies that the Buddha rescues and benefits those suffering from the pains of birth and illness.
While dwelling in the womb, one goes and stays with the mother, moving east and west in silent darkness, suffering alone; though the family members are around, who among them can truly know this?
If the mother drinks too much, her body swells and heaves.
If the mother drinks but little, the hungry intestines become constricted.
If the mother walks hurriedly, her neck becomes as thin as a rope.
If the mother sits still, her body feels as if weighed down by a mountain, and she lacks any radiance.
Like the Black Darkness Hell,
one cannot move about;
like the Iron Net Hell, [one is bound].
If the mother drinks something hot, it is like the Hell of Boiling Water;
if she drinks something cold, it is like the Hell of Cold Ice.
Only after undergoing various sufferings for fifteen hundred years at the edge [of her womb] does she finally emerge.
The suffering of birth is moreover difficult to conceive.
At the moment of birth, the body is enveloped by the amniotic sac;
it is like being bound, with blood flowing over the flesh—what is this different from being flayed upon a mountain of blades? It is as if falling onto straw after having been skinned.
The wind comes and blows upon the body;
if the cold ice cuts into the flesh, one loses voice without even realizing it.

It is as if a thousand chisels were vying to carve one's spirit, leaving the mind desolate and dark; the inner being is ruined and obscured, such that one is unaware of the existence of heaven and earth.
They were unaware of the sun and moon;
they were unaware of their parents;
they were unaware of their elder brothers and sisters.
Constantly suffering from much pain, they cry out without ceasing.
For two or three years, they gradually cease nursing; although their physical bodies grow long, their mental consciousness remains clouded.
Seeing water, they immediately throw themselves in and die without realizing it;
they cast their bodies into fire;
and one cannot discern who it is that draws a knife to stab themselves, wailing in lamentation.
They fall from great heights without any sense of fear;
they crawl along the roads and do not know how to return;
they encounter wolves and pass tigers without giving rise to terror or timidity.
This birth is indeed suffering and is truly difficult to endure.
As for the suffering of old age: when things flourish, they must inevitably decline; when one reaches the prime of life, one must inevitably grow old.
This matter is clear; its verification is as plain as looking at one's own palm.
Therefore, those with black hair, like spokes remaining on a wheel, are driven away by hair that has become empty.
The flush of youth is but temporarily entrusted to this body and will surely be usurped by the white eyebrows of old age;
once the pathways of vitality are slightly severed, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) become entirely empty,
and the sinews and marrow gradually wither away.
Whom did these four limbs belong?
They have thus caused the eyes to clear of double pus and the ears to open from their two obstructions.
The nose does not smell fragrances;
the tongue loses the sense of sweet and pungent;
the body no longer perceives touch.
The consciousness is clouded and deluded, the hair is disheveled,
the teeth have fallen out,
the waist is bent, and the back is hunched; every step taken is a slow inch, and his speech is unintelligible.
Yet who among the youthful and heroic now knows of those empty paths?
That former splendor—where is it now?
Even if one were to set up a lofty carriage on the road, the entry to the gate would forever be cut off.

Facing a swift steed, one finally parts from the urge to mount and leap; beholding a pure vessel, the heart harbors no longing or envy. When the songs of Shun fill the courtyard, how could one cast a glance even at the Emperor’s eyes?

In former days, Zhuangzi lived out his years indulging his desires and did not cultivate even the slightest merit; as he now approaches the path of the underworld, he still shows no sign of repentance.
Once one has fallen into the mire of the defilements, it is difficult to emerge even with renewed effort.
For those suffering from illness, the calamities of the three poisons pervade the world, and the pains of the four elements converge intensely upon Jambudvīpa.
Yet, according to whether one's karma is high or low, the retribution is likewise light or heavy.
Some may be robust and vigorous at dawn, yet in a mere moment illness gathers;
thus they are made to suffer from chronic dysentery for years and be entangled by goiters for ages.
Or, worms bore through their bones, and white nodes connect them.
Pus flows out onto the skin of the four limbs and the joints;
the abdomen becomes as large as a drum,
while the head becomes pointed like a锥 (chui/awl).
Their cries resound through the streets and their stench fills the gates.
Some have swollen and curled hands and feet;
others have sores and ulcers on their waists and backs that they can only move with difficulty, like mountains rising at every step.
Their bodies and arms become as hard as iron;
they may suffer from chills in winter or pestilence in summer,
experiencing sudden heat and sudden cold until their lives are as precarious as a flash of lightning, and their labored breathing is like being cut off.
Some encounter various poisons where tendons are severed from flesh; they long for life but cannot find it, and though they seek death, there is no way to do so.
Some suffer from parching heat or freezing cold as their five viscera are torn apart; they drink pus for years and vomit blood for successive years.
Ulcers break out in competition along the galleries of the body, and carbuncles emerge in rivalry; the neck becomes as thin as a thread, and the face swells like a sack.
Sometimes blood flows from the eyes and pus issues from both ears;
though heaven and earth are vast, one can see nothing clearly.
As if thunder were splitting the mountains, he remained unaware;
his hands rested upon a damp bed, and he could not sleep in peace.
His mouth craved strange gruel, and he was constantly reduced to a mere skeleton.
Some are deranged and confused, their consciousness clouded by folly;
they enter the water as if returning home or rush into fire without realizing it.
Others have mouths closed like pincers and tongues stiff as stone.
They nod their heads to speak and move their eyes to converse;
sometimes a snake within the brain is removed only for it to emerge again, or two demons in the heart pierce them,
only for them to arise once more in such a manner.
The suffering of illness is inconceivable;
though one may have exquisite celestial delicacies, they are no different from iron balls,
and the sugarcane on earth is more bitter than molten copper.
Beneficent deities do not grant protection, while malevolent spirits press in from all sides.
The bed emits flames so that one cannot sleep; though one desires to warm oneself at the hearth, there is no way to sit by it.
Such various ailments are indeed great suffering. As for the suffering of death:
Indeed, for those living in this transient world to merely chant that their lives span a full hundred years is ultimately a fallacious claim, as their lifespans are inconsistent and varied;
some perish in the womb, some waste away in the prime of youth,
and others meet their end within the privacy of their own homes.
Some were executed by the sword in the marketplace;
some had their feet severed at the river-crossing;
others hanged themselves in the desolate valleys.
Some had their bodies torn apart by five chariots;
some had their remains divided among the four quarters;
some entered the water and encountered crocodiles.
Some wandered the mountains and encountered tigers;
some were amidst the ashes while listening to the fire;
some harbored purity yet suffered from hunger.
Furthermore, as causes and conditions are entangled and karmic retributions are disparate, though one speaks of a hundred-year lifespan, who can enjoy even a single portion of it?
Thus, before the sound of laughter has ceased, the cry of weeping is already heard; and before the celebratory countenance has shifted, the mournful guests have already arrived.

Consequently, embroidered screens are covered in dust and carved steps are overgrown with weeds; singing halls gather wild beasts and dancing pavilions harbor birds. One harbors doubts regarding one's own chamber and feels dread looking toward the empty spirit.
Thus, those who receive the resonance of the mind immediately perceive enemies, while those who have been close since childhood appear as strangers.

Thus they become a repository of enmity; in their ordinary times, they may hasten to the vermilion halls with tinkling steps or dwell with composed grace in the purple chambers, shaking jade pendants against white skirts and reflecting golden hairpins upon their hanging necks.
Their hearts are captivated by honor, and their official ambitions soar above the clouds.
Who would have thought that one might depart from a lofty hall only to sink into a grave mound at dusk, where their physical remains are devoured by ants and their souls are seized by the hells?
Thereupon, the tips of blades pierce their backs, sword edges penetrate their chests, iron pythons coil around their waists, and bronze serpents wind about their bones.
Long pincers pull out their tongues, and sharp nails pierce their eyes;
cold ice penetrates to the marrow, and hot coals sear the skin.
Consequently, their sinews are crushed between the teeth of saws, and blood flows beyond the grinding beds.
Alternatively, their five viscera are stretched out along the edges of the saws,
and their four limbs are suspended from the hooks;
as the ox-headed, eight-cornered saws touch the flesh until it falls away into ash, the hell-wardens’ four fangs crush the brains until they are putrid and decayed.

Even if one were to eat iron for many consecutive years, it would not alleviate chronic hunger; though one may long for copper throughout kalpas, how could one know it would save one from eternal thirst?
This suffering is indeed difficult to endure. Therefore, one should resolve to awaken the mind and vow to practice the twelve vows.
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*,
this refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta.
There are four types of arousing the mind.
First, the resolve born of great compassion;
second, the resolve to protect the Dharma;
third, the resolve born from contemplating the faults and afflictions of the body.
Fourth is the generation of the mind seeking the most supreme fruit.
Regarding the generation of the mind through great compassion:
one contemplates that sentient beings in the six realms are all bound by fetters.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta.
In the hells, there is the suffering of undergoing punishment;
among animals, there is the suffering of mutual predation.
The hungry ghosts suffer the misery of hunger;
the gods suffer the misery of decline;
and among human beings, there is the misery of seeking and desiring.
In the heavens, there is the suffering of the exhaustion of karmic retribution.
Observing these sentient beings, all submerged in the ocean of suffering,
they seek benefit yet do not know the way out.
"I now resolve my mind with the desire to fully realize and uproot [suffering];
this is called the generation of the mind of great compassion. Second is the generation of the mind for protecting the Dharma.
There are three kinds of Dharma.
This refers to principle, teaching, and practice.
The Dharma is eternal; however, there are times of penetration and obstruction, and there is the concealment and manifestation of human action.
Or, encountering an era of decline when the true teaching gradually fades away,
empty words flow alongside guest-teachings,
and perilous paths vie with dream-tracks for passage.
The various doctrines were as chaotic as heterodox views competing with one another; the holy teachings were intermingled and oppressed, such that the true path was nearly lost in disorder.
The Bodhisattva then thought:
"My teacher is the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
Having undergone various hardships and austerities throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
you have gathered this Dharma-treasure, desiring that it remain long in the world to benefit all sentient beings through the Path.
How can it now suddenly be known to sink into oblivion?
I now resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of protecting the Dharma, not begrudging even my body or life.
I desire that the Great Way, though obscured, may be made manifest once more; I wish to awaken those in this world of darkness so that all beings in the world may obtain the eye of right view.
This is called the bodhisattva’s resolve to protect the Dharma. Third, regarding the resolve arising from contemplating the body as encountering affliction:
the bodhisattva reflects, "This body of mine is truly a dwelling place for birth, old age, sickness, and death."
The body is a thicket of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness;
the body is the source from which affliction arises, and the mind is the master that perceives suffering.
For ten months in the womb, one dwells together with impurity, and such is the case at birth as well.
Thus, it is a collection of manifold sufferings:
either the pain of illness that is so acute as to be incessant day and night;
or the suffering of being separated from those one loves and encountering those one hates; or the frustration, vexation, and anguish of failing to obtain what one seeks.
Or their food and clothing may be insufficient.

Thus, from dawn until dusk, they briefly contemplate the eight [sufferings]: birth, old age, sickness, death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Cycling through the six realms of existence, they undergo these sufferings without knowing their limit.

If one does not feel weary of them and seek liberation, by what means could one escape these present hardships? Now that I have resolved my mind [upon awakening], though these manifold sufferings are difficult to leave, I shall leave them; and though the unsurpassed holy path is difficult to attain, I shall realize it.
This is called the arousal of the mind through contemplating the faults and afflictions of the body. Fourth, regarding the arousal of the mind seeking the most supreme fruit:
the bodies of all Buddhas are equal and are of two kinds.
The first is the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
His feet were endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
he was so upright, dignified,
and extraordinary that there was no peer to him in the world, and even sentient beings with evil hearts would become harmonious and joyful upon seeing him.
How much more so for those who hear the good— how could they look upon it and find no benefit?
Second is the Dharma-body,
which fills the entire Dharma-realm.

He is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes.
This one seeks liberation from the hunger, thirst, cold, and heat of birth and death.

To sever the entanglements of the six realms and renounce the defilements of the five stages of abiding is precisely the profound aspiration for which students bend their necks in reverence and resolve their minds; this is truly due to the relative lightness or gravity of what is being abandoned.
This is called the generation of the mind seeking the most supreme fruit, which causes all sentient beings to obtain whatever they seek.
Below this is the third section, which concludes both the practices and the vows. As for the first vow:
In this section of the formal exposition below,
the second stage— the single, extensive vow— likewise aims to eliminate that which has not yet been attained, clarifying the meaning of the Buddha-fruit;
for although it is already present [in potential], there is a reason to seek it through aspiration because it has not yet been realized.
Regarding the sequence of aspiration, practice, and vow, these three are simultaneous; however, from the perspective of principle, one first aspires and later practices.
As for the latter [the sequence of practice followed by aspiration], how is this known?
It is commonly said that while the vow is vast when contemplated, it is full when put into practice; thus, it clarifies that the vow comes first and practice follows.
Within the clarification of the vow, there are two major divisions.
The first is the essence of the vow.
The second section establishes the vows to induce the purchase;
subsequently, within the initial clarification of the vows, there are twelve vows in total,
which are now arranged as six pairs.
First, seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above constitutes one pair;
second, merit and wisdom constitute one pair;
third, self-cultivation and the transformation of others constitute one pair.
The fourth constitutes a pair based on the essence of compassion;
the fifth constitutes a pair consisting of subduing the great māras and converting non-Buddhists;
and the sixth constitutes a pair based on the objects of compassion.
Now, setting aside the latter for the moment, within the first pair itself, they do not distinguish themselves as two different things.
Why? Because the first vow is the aspiration to become a Buddha in an impure land, while the second vow is the aspiration to become a Buddha in a pure land.
These two vows constitute the body that is the virtuous and excellent fruit of enlightenment.
Within the first [vow], regarding the body sought in an impure land, there is further a threefold division.
First is the enumeration of the number.
The second is the arousal of the vow;
the third is the dedication of merit to sentient beings.
"The first vow" indicates the enumeration. "May I, in future lives... [and so forth].
The second is to give rise to the aspiration that all sentient beings may be no different from oneself.
The third is the dedication of merit to sentient beings.
Regarding the second aspiration:
This is the vow to become a Buddha in a Pure Land.
Within this vow, there are generally three distinct parts.
The first indicates the number.
The second is the arousal of the aspiration;
the third is the bestowing [of it] upon sentient beings.
As for the second aspiration:
First, the enumeration of the number establishes my aspiration for future lives.
Within this aspiration, it is further divided into two parts;
first, the primary request for the fruits of future retribution.
The second seeks the fruit of future cultivation.
One’s own body is like pure lapis lazuli, free from all blemish;
is this not the body of the Pure Land?
The substance of lapis lazuli is pure;
likewise, the body of the Pure Land is a body of emptiness and non-substantiality, an infinitely vast essence.
Its merit and virtue are towering and sublime.
This second section clarifies the fruit of the excellent cultivation of bodhi.
Just as the sun illuminates the world, it clarifies the fruit of the cultivation of wisdom;
all sentient beings dwelling in darkness and obscurity receive its enlightening revelation.
The third is the bestowing of gifts upon sentient beings.
As for this third vow,
this pair clarifies the adornment of merit and the adornment of wisdom.
This is the adornment of wisdom.
These two adornments are explained extensively in separate chapters;
they should be discussed in full detail here.
However, for now, let us explain its name.
Its "merit" (guṇa) is also called "blessing" (puṇya).
"Blessing" refers to beneficial welfare.
It is well able to provide supplementary support;
because it brings benefit and merit to the practitioner, it is called "merit" (puṇya).
Because this merit is the virtue residing in wholesome conduct, it is termed "meritorious virtue" (puṇyaguṇa).
Just as clarity, coolness, and so forth are the qualities (*guṇa*) belonging to water,
"merit" (*guṇa*) refers to functional capacity (*śakti*).
Because wholesome states possess the capacity to provide support, nourishment, and benefit, they are called "merit."
This merit is called "merit" (*guṇa*) because it is the virtue residing in wholesome conduct.
Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*): according to the Abhidharma, that which performs decisive discernment is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
this is in contrast to the various types of "patience" (*kṣānti*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
because there is no attachment to the distinct conceptualizations of names and cognitions,
one understands phenomena through their common characteristics; this is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and discernment (*prajñā*):

this wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*prajñā*) are explained as referring to a single entity, yet they are distinguished separately according to their respective meanings; there is no lack of difference between them.
What are their specific characteristics?
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, knowing conventional truth is called wisdom (*jñāna*),
while knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is designated as insight (*prajñā*).
Therefore, his words state that the partial knowledge of all phenomena is called the *jñānapāramitā*,
while the awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Nirvana is likewise.
If one relies on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to establish that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called "conformity to knowledge" (*jñānānuvartin*),
then the thorough comprehension of the teachings is called "conformity to wisdom" (*prajñānuvartin*).
All shall remain unhurt.
In these two sūtras, this is termed "ornamentation" (vyūha) and is also termed "restraint" (saṃvara).
It is also called the "auxiliary dharma," and it is further described as "bodhi.
To speak fully, it is termed "adornment."
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
it is called "ornamentation" because it can adorn the practitioner;
furthermore, the mutual adorning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is also called "ornamentation."
Just as an ornament is interspersed with various jewels, so it is with restraint (*saṃvara*).
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "Restraint" refers to [the discipline of] the Bodhisattva.
Because these two are internally regulated, they are called "vinaya" (discipline).
It is the standard for conforming to the Dharma, like a scale or a ritual procedure.
As for what is called "aiding the Dharma":
Speaking in terms of looking toward the fruit, because it serves as a support that accords with bodhi, it is called an "auxiliary dharma" (dharmasahāya).
Because it can act as the cause for Buddhahood,
it is further described as "bodhi."
May I fully bring the Buddha-way to accomplishment in future lives.
First, I vow that my pursuit of the Buddha-way shall be lofty and magnificent.
Second, I vow that once I have attained Buddhahood, I shall be adorned with merit and wisdom—this is what is meant by "lofty and magnificent."
This clarifies that the adornment of merit illuminates the world.
These four characters distinguish the practitioner of the adornment of wisdom;
it refers to the third stage of the path of vision, wherein one bestows gifts upon sentient beings below.
The fifth vow consists of the following two sections,
which form a pair comprising both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
First is self-cultivation.
Regarding the clarification of one's own practice, there are only two sections:
first, the indication of the number;
second, the arousal of the vow.
The fifth vow: First, the enumeration;
[it is] to arouse great diligence.
The second aspiration:
In the past, there was a great *piyāla* tree inhabited by many birds and beasts. A wild fire broke out and burned from three sides simultaneously;
only one side was separated by a body of water. The animals were driven to the brink of exhaustion, with no place left to escape for their lives.
At that time, I was a large-bodied, powerful deer;
with my forelegs spanning one bank and my hind legs bracing the other bank.
He allowed the various beasts to tread upon his back as they crossed over;
though his skin and flesh were completely ruined,
he endured it through the power of his compassion.
Upon reaching the very end of his life,
a single rabbit arrived; though his strength was utterly exhausted, he exerted himself with fierce resolve and managed to let it pass over him.
His back broke, he fell into the water, and died. Within this vow, there are two distinct parts:
the first clarifies the beginning of observing the precepts; the second clarifies the end of observing the precepts.
The initial resolve and self-vow mark the beginning of clearly upholding the precepts.
As for why the precepts are called "ground," a sutra states:
"They may serve as level ground capable of producing all manner of virtues; the sutras and precepts are not transgressed."
This clarifies the conclusion of upholding the precepts.
As for the sixth vow,
this clarifies the outward transformation of sentient beings who are blind or deaf.
The blindness of these individuals is due to grave sins committed in previous lives,
such as destroying the eyes of sentient beings or gouging out the eyes of sentient beings.
If one is blind because of having destroyed the eye of right view,
then even one who steals jewels or lamps from a stūpa is likewise blind.
For what reason and by what causes is one deaf?
The answer is: Because one received the teacher’s civil instruction and admonition but did not accept or practice it, instead responding with anger, one becomes deaf.
Furthermore, it is due to cutting off the ears of sentient beings, piercing the ears of sentient beings, or stealing items from the stūpas of the Buddha or the monastic community.
Furthermore, one becomes deaf because of stealing the bells from a *gandhārī* drum.
One becomes mute because in a previous life one cut off another’s tongue, or stuffed their mouth,
or gave them a harmful drug so that they could not speak.
Or, having heard the instructions of a teacher or the words of one's parents, one does not follow them; because one speaks of what is wrong, one becomes mute.
As for the insane: they disturb those practicing *dhyāna*, and those who disturb practitioners of *dhyāna* are swallowed [by the earth].
It is like a Brahmin who, having lost his rice field and then seeing his wife die, immediately goes mad and runs about naked.
Furthermore, for example, there was the bhikṣuṇī Ciñcā-Kauṇḍinya.
When she was still a laywoman, her seven sons all died;
because of her great grief and sorrow, she lost her mind and went mad, becoming naked.
Question: Previously it was said that the insane attain sanity; now it is said that the naked obtain clothing. Since madness has been removed, how can there still be nakedness?
Answer: There are two kinds of madness.
The first is that which everyone knows to be madness.
Second, because of evil and perverse views, one is naked oneself yet does not realize one is insane.
As it is said, there was once a Dharma master in the country of South India who sat upon a high seat and preached the meaning of the five precepts.
Many non-Buddhists came among the sentient beings to listen.
The king then raised an objection, saying:
"If it is as you have described..."
If someone gives alcohol as a gift or drinks it themselves, they will receive the retribution of being deluded, insane, and foolish.
Consequently, among the people of the present age, those who ought to be insane are many while those who are sane are few;
yet now, those who are insane are few while those who are not insane are many.
Why was this so? At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners said, "Excellent!
This challenge is most profound."
"This bald-headed man will certainly be unable to answer when called upon to speak aloud;
for the King possesses sharp intelligence.
At that time, the Dharma Master pointed his finger at the various non-Buddhists and spoke further, elaborating on other matters.
The king then immediately understood the words of the various non-Buddhists. The non-Buddhists said to the king:
"The king's question is exceedingly profound;
we do not know how to answer it."
Ashamed of his ignorance, he merely raised his finger and spoke of other matters.
The King said to the heretic seated on the high throne: "Having finished answering with your finger, you must now protect and uphold [the truth]."
It is not by mere words that I say this; I am telling you that you are mad, and your madness is no small matter.
You smear your bodies with ashes, you are shameless in your appearance, and you eat filth from human skulls.
Tearing out one's hair, lying upon thorns, hanging by the nose, entering the water in winter, or being scorched by fire in summer—
such various practices that are not the Way are all signs of madness.
It is because the Dharma Master, wishing to protect you, pointed it out but did not explain it.
This is called "naked madness.
According to the sutras and treatises, one cannot obtain even a small portion of what people practice.
In the past, there were two brothers who left the household life to seek the Way.
One maintained the precepts, recited the sutras, and practiced seated meditation;
the other sought out donors extensively to cultivate various meritorious deeds.
Upon the appearance of Śākyamuni Buddha in the world,
one was born into the family of an elder,
while the other became a great white elephant with the strength to defeat enemies.
The elder left the household life to study the Way and attained the six supernormal powers as an arhat;
however, due to his meager merit, it was difficult for him to obtain almsfood while begging.
One day, carrying his bowl to beg for food throughout the city, he was unable to find anything and arrived at the stable of the white elephant, where he saw the king’s offerings.
The elephant was abundant in various [provisions].
He spoke to this elephant, saying:
"Both you and I are equally guilty and oppressed."
The elephant was immediately overcome with grief and did not eat for three days.
The elephant-keeper, filled with fear, sought out the practitioner;
upon seeing him, he asked, "What sorcery have you employed to cause the King’s white elephant to fall ill and be unable to eat?"
He replied,
"This elephant was my younger brother during a previous life.
Together with me, he left the household life to seek the Way at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha."
"I merely observe the precepts, recite the sūtras, and practice seated meditation, but I do not practice giving.
My younger brother merely seeks out donors extensively to perform various meritorious deeds and practices giving, but he does not observe the precepts nor does he study."
Question: Because he did not observe the precepts, recite the sutras, or practice meditation, he has now become this elephant;
because he extensively practiced giving, his food and drink are fully provided and all manner of things are abundant.
"Because I practiced only the Way and did not cultivate generosity,
although I have now attained the Way, I am unable to obtain alms when begging for food.
For this reason, the causes and conditions are different."
Regarding those who recover from illness:
there are two kinds of illness.
The first is internal illness, wherein the five viscera are disordered, resulting in chronic knots and latent ailments.
Second, there are external illnesses such as being trampled by galloping horses, falling from heights, or injuries from weapons, blades, and staves;
there are also those illnesses resulting from past karma. A question is asked: [What is the cause?]
By what causes and conditions does one contract this illness?
The answer is:
because in previous lives one took pleasure in inflicting various afflictions, such as using whips and staves, torturing, beating, binding, and imprisoning.
In this present life, one contracts illnesses; in this very life, one does not know how to care for the body, being immoderate in food and drink and irregular in sleeping and rising.
Due to these matters, one contracts various kinds of diseases.
Thus, there are four hundred and four such illnesses.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he causes the sick to be healed and those with physical disabilities to become whole.
What is meant by "physical disability"?
It refers to someone who, in a previous life, injured another's body by cutting off their head or severing their hands and feet.
Or, because they have damaged images of the Buddha or their parents,
they may suffer from physical deformities or incomplete limbs; yet, by receiving the great grace of the Buddha,
they all attain full restoration.
For example, within the Jetavana Monastery, there was a young man named Rurujyotiṣka—translated in the Qin language as "the nephew of King Prasenajit.
He was handsome, brave, and strong, with a naturally gentle and kind disposition. When the king’s principal consort saw him, she became infatuated with him and summoned him in secret.
He wished to compel her to comply with him, but she utterly refused.
The lady became greatly incensed and slandered him to the king, even turning his virtues into crimes.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately had him dismembered limb by limb and cast away among the burial mounds.
Before his life had even ceased,
that night tigers, wolves, and rākṣasas came intending to devour him.
At that moment, the Buddha arrived at his side and illuminated him with his radiance.
His body immediately became healed and at ease;
his mind was filled with great joy.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him.
He then attained the three paths.
The Buddha took pity on him and led him by the hand to the Jetavana Monastery.
This man said, "My body has already been broken and discarded; may the Buddha restore my body."
"Now, for the remainder of this life, I shall give my body as an offering. On the following day,
King Prasenajit heard of these matters and came to the Jeta Grove.
Huan spoke to Jian, speaking most earnestly of his past remorse:
"You truly have no fault; it was unjust for me to harm you through comparison.
Now I shall divide the kingdom with you and rule half of it together."
Gandaka said, "I too am weary of this;
the King is likewise without fault."
"This is the retribution for the calamities and various offenses committed by me in past lives.
Now that I have offered my own body to the Buddha and the Sangha, it shall not be returned.
Thus, if there are sentient beings who are incomplete [in their faculties],"
Having received the Buddha’s radiance, one attains fulfillment.

the two vows below constitute a pair based on the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*).

by virtue of the causes and conditions of my wholesome karma, become the foremost one to emerge from the realm of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings who have committed immeasurable evil deeds.

may I, in future lives, give rise to the aspiration that if there are those who are poor, destitute, or naked, [I shall provide for them].
